'''Jack Howard Silver''' (23 April 1942 – 22 December 2016<ref>Group in Logic and the Methodology of Science, "[http://logic.berkeley.edu/news.html Jack Howard Silver]", University of California&ndash;Berkeley</ref>) was an American [[set theorist]] and [[logician]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. Silver made several contributions to set theory in the areas of [[large cardinal]]s and the [[constructible universe]] ''L''.

== Early life ==
Born in Montana, he earned his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in Mathematics at Berkeley in 1966 under [[Robert Lawson Vaught|Robert Vaught]]<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=22309}}</ref> before taking a position at the same institution the following year. He held an [[Sloan Fellowship|Alfred P. Sloan Research Fellowship]] from 1970 to 1972. 

== Contributions ==

In his 1975 paper "On the Singular Cardinals Problem", Silver [[mathematical proof|proved]] that if a [[cardinal number|cardinal]] ''κ'' is [[singular cardinal|singular]] with [[uncountable]] [[cofinality]] and 2<sup>''λ''</sup> = ''λ''<sup>+</sup> for all infinite cardinals ''λ'' < ''κ'', then 2<sup>''κ''</sup> = ''κ''<sup>+</sup>. Prior to Silver's proof, many mathematicians believed that a [[forcing (mathematics)|forcing]] argument would yield that the negation of the theorem is [[consistency|consistent]] with [[ZFC]]. He introduced the notion of a ''master condition'', which became an important tool in forcing proofs involving large cardinals.<ref>Cummings, James (2009). "Iterated Forcing and Elementary Embeddings". In ''Handbook of Set Theory'', Springer, pp.&nbsp;775–883, esp. pp.&nbsp;814ff.</ref>

Silver proved the consistency of [[Chang's conjecture]] using the Silver collapse (which is a variation of the [[List_of_forcing_notions#Levy_collapsing|Levy collapse]]). He proved that, assuming the consistency of a [[supercompact cardinal]], it is possible to construct a model where 2<sup>''κ''</sup> = ''κ''<sup>++</sup> holds for some [[measurable cardinal]] ''κ''. With the introduction of the so-called [[Silver machine]]s he was able to give a fine structure free proof of [[Ronald Jensen|Jensen's]] [[covering lemma]]. He is also credited with discovering [[Silver indiscernible]]s and generalizing the notion of a [[Kurepa tree]] (called Silver's Principle). He discovered [[zero sharp|0#]] ("zero sharp") in his 1966 Ph.D. thesis, discussed in the graduate textbook ''Set Theory: An Introduction to Large Cardinals'' by Frank R. Drake.<ref>Drake, F. R. (1974). "Set Theory: An Introduction to Large Cardinals". ''Studies in Logic and the Foundations of Mathematics'' 76, Elsevier. {{ISBN|0-444-10535-2}}</ref>

Silver's original work involving large cardinals was perhaps motivated by the goal of showing the inconsistency of an uncountable measurable cardinal; instead he was led to discover indiscernibles in ''L'' assuming a measurable cardinal exists.

== Selected publications ==
<!-- list from https://math.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/jack-h-silver --> 
*Silver, Jack H. (1971). "Some applications of model theory in set theory". ''Annals of Mathematical Logic'' '''3'''(1), pp.&nbsp;45–110.
*Silver, Jack H. (1973). "The bearing of large cardinals on constructibility". In ''Studies in Model Theory'', MAA Studies in Mathematics 8, pp.&nbsp;158–182.
*Silver, Jack H. (1974). "Indecomposable ultrafilters and 0#". In ''Proceedings of the Tarski Symposium'', Proceedings of Symposia in Pure Mathematics XXV, pp.&nbsp;357–363.
*Silver, Jack (1975). "On the singular cardinals problem". In ''Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians'' 1, pp.&nbsp;265–268.
*Silver, Jack H. (1980). "Counting the number of equivalence classes of Borel and coanalytic equivalence relations". ''Annals of Mathematical Logic'' '''18'''(1), pp.&nbsp;1–28.
